label: The Twelve — Part 2 — Yoel and Amos
summary_plain: Yoel describes a devastating locust invasion — the land stripped bare, the grain offering and drink offering cut off from the house of YHWH. Blow the shofar in Tziyon! YHWH promises to pour out his ruach on all flesh — your sons and daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions. Even on the male and female servants I will pour out my ruach. YHWH will gather all the nations and bring them down to the Valley of Yehoshafat and enter into judgment with them there on account of my people Yisra'EL. Amos — a herdsman from Teqoa — declares YHWH's roar from Tziyon against the nations. For three transgressions and for four. YHWH demands justice: let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream. You who turn justice to wormwood and cast down righteousness to the earth. YHWH says: I hate, I despise your festivals — I take no delight in your solemn assemblies. But let justice roll down.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the Minor Prophets Scroll (4QXII, 8HevXIIgr, and Murabba'at) and the Orit Ge'ez. Yoel's ruach-pouring prophecy (2:28-29/3:1-2 in the Hebrew) is among the most significant in the prophetic literature — YHWH's ruach poured out on all flesh regardless of gender or social status, including servants. Acts 2 cites this passage at Pentecost, but the original text promises prophetic empowerment to all covenant people — not the establishment of a new institution. Amos is the foundational social justice prophet. His background — a herdsman, not a professional prophet (7:14) — establishes that prophetic authority comes from YHWH's call, not institutional training. The judgment formula 'for three transgressions and for four' covers Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moav, Yehudah, and Yisra'EL — YHWH judges all nations by the same standard of justice.

key_terms.definition: The shortest book among the prophets; a single-chapter oracle pronouncing YHWH's judgment against Edom for its pride and its betrayal of Yisra'el in the day of disaster.
YHWH's decree against Edom (descendants of Esav): their mountain fortress pride will be brought down; as they did to Yisra'el they will receive in return.
A prophet who fled from YHWH's commission to warn Nineveh; swallowed by a great fish; and ultimately confronted with YHWH's compassion extending beyond Yisra'el.
YHWH appointed a great fish to swallow Yonah for three days and three nights after he was thrown overboard. This ancient text is the source; NT writers borrowed the sign of Yonah's three days.
The entire city of Nineveh — king, people, and animals — fasted and turned from violence when Yonah's warning reached them, and YHWH relented from the announced judgment.

YHWH challenges Yonah's anger at divine compassion: 'Should I not be concerned about Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left?'
A prophet from Moresheth who addressed both the northern and southern kingdoms; his oracles include sharp social justice indictments and famous summations of what YHWH requires.
YHWH's answer to what covenant faithfulness requires: 'to do justice, to love kindness, and to walk humbly with YHWH your Creator.'
YHWH announces a ruler will come from Beit-Lekhem of Yehudah, whose origins are from of old. Ancient source text; NT writers borrowed from Mikhah 5:2.
A prophet whose name means 'comfort'; his entire book is an oracle of YHWH's judgment against Nineveh — the same city Yonah warned a generation earlier; this time no repentance comes.

faq.question: What is the book of Ovadyah about and why is it significant?
faq.answer: Ovadyah is the shortest book in the Hebrew prophetic collection — a single chapter oracle against Edom. Its significance lies in the accountability principle: Edom had stood by while Yisra'el suffered, even assisting enemies, and YHWH announces that every deed returns on its doer's own head.

faq.question: Why did Yonah flee from YHWH's commission to go to Nineveh?
faq.answer: The book itself reveals the reason only at the end: Yonah knew that YHWH is compassionate and slow to anger, and he feared that if Nineveh repented, YHWH would relent from judgment. He fled to Tarshish rather than be an instrument of mercy toward an enemy nation.

faq.question: What is the significance of the great fish in Yonah's story?
faq.answer: YHWH appointed the fish as the instrument of rescue — not punishment. Yonah was swallowed when thrown overboard and prayed from inside the fish (Yonah ch.2). The three days and three nights inside the fish is the ancient text; NT writers borrowed this imagery for their invented figure's burial claim. The original is about YHWH's rescue of Yonah.

faq.question: How did Nineveh's response in Yonah 3 demonstrate genuine repentance?
faq.answer: When Yonah's warning reached Nineveh, the entire city — from the king on his throne to the lowest person — fasted, put on sackcloth, and turned from violence. The king issued a decree commanding the city to call earnestly to YHWH. YHWH saw their turning and relented from the announced judgment.

faq.question: Why was Yonah angry at YHWH's compassion in chapter 4?
faq.answer: Yonah was angry because YHWH's mercy toward Nineveh felt unjust to him. He had declared the city would be overthrown in forty days, and when it was not, his prophetic message seemed to have failed. YHWH's response — 'Should I not be concerned about 120,000 people?' — rebukes prophetic nationalism over divine compassion.

faq.question: What is Mikhah 6:8 and why is it considered one of the most important covenant statements?
faq.answer: Mikhah 6:8 is YHWH's direct answer to what the covenant truly demands: do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with YHWH your Creator. It strips away all religious performance and reduces covenant faithfulness to three inseparable things: righteous action, loyal love, and humble relationship — all under YHWH's authority, not human institutions.

faq.question: What ancient text does Mikhah 5:2 contain and what did NT writers do with it?
faq.answer: Mikhah 5:2 announces that from Beit-Lekhem of Yehudah a ruler will emerge for Yisra'el, whose origins are from ancient days. This is an ancient Hebrew covenant text about Yehudah's future ruler. NT writers borrowed this text to construct the birth narrative for the invented figure; the original ancient source predates that borrowing by centuries.

faq.question: How does Nakhum's oracle against Nineveh differ from Yonah's?
faq.answer: Yonah's generation saw Nineveh repent and YHWH relent. By Nakhum's time, Nineveh's empire had become the terror of the ancient world under the Assyrian empire. Nakhum's oracle announces YHWH's coming judgment against the city with no call to repentance — the time for that has passed.

faq.question: What does Mikhah 4:3 envision for the future and how does it compare to Yoel 3:10?
faq.answer: Mikhah 4:3 (also found nearly identically in Yesha'yahu 2:4) describes a future age of peace where weapons are beaten into agricultural tools — swords into plowshares, spears into pruning hooks. Yoel 3:10 deliberately reverses this image, calling the nations to arm themselves for battle. Both are authentic ancient texts; the reversal is deliberate prophetic tension.

faq.question: What is the lasting impact of the book of Yonah on Hebrew covenant understanding?
faq.answer: Yonah confronts the assumption that YHWH's compassion is the exclusive property of Yisra'el. YHWH is not a tribal deity but the Creator whose concern extends to Nineveh's 120,000 inhabitants and their animals. The book also documents a prophet who fled and failed — and YHWH's purposes were accomplished anyway.
